learning_objective: 🎯 Learn how to design and create a magical mini-ecosystem right in your school that gives a safe home to birds, butterflies, and friendly insects!

main_concepts.simple_explanation: A habitat garden is not just for looking pretty; it is built to be a living home! It provides three essential things for local wildlife: food, clean water, and safe shelter for birds, frogs, and friendly bugs.

Bees, butterflies, and small birds are called pollinators. As they fly from flower to flower drinking nectar, they move pollen around, which helps plants grow fruits and seeds. Without them, our food supply would be in big trouble!

Native plants are the trees and bushes that naturally grow in your city or region. Local insects and birds are already used to them, and they require much less water and zero chemical fertilizers to survive.
To make a great habitat, you need layers! Tall trees for birds to nest, low shrubs for hiding, and a shallow clay bowl of fresh water (a birdbath) for thirsty creatures to drink and splash around in.

fun_activity.title: 🦋 The Butterfly Spotter Challenge!
fun_activity.instructions: Spend 10 minutes in your school garden or a local park. Count how many different types of butterflies or bees you can spot, and sketch the flower they visited most often!

quick_recap: ⭐ A habitat garden provides food, water, and shelter to local wildlife.
⭐ Pollinators like bees and butterflies are essential for plants to produce seeds and fruits.
⭐ Native plants are the best choice because they are perfectly adapted to the local weather.
⭐ Creating layers of tall and short plants helps different animals find their perfect hiding spots.
⭐ Setting up a simple birdbath is an easy way to attract thirsty birds to your garden.
